title: Meland, Sigurd N, Own Motion Order
text:
74 Van Natta 1 (2022) 1
In the Matter of the Compensation of
SIGURD N. MELAND, Claimant
Own Motion No. 21-00024OM
OWN MOTION ORDER REVIEWING CARRIER CLOSURE
Unrepresented Claimant
Reinisch Wilson Weier PC, Defense Attorneys
Reviewing Panel: Members Ousey and Curey.
Claimant, pro se,1 requests review of a June 23, 2020, Own Motion Notice
of Closure that did not award permanent disability benefits for his “post-
aggravation rights” new/omitted medical condition (left knee anterior cruciate
ligament (ACL) tear).2 Based on the following reasoning, we modify the closure
notice.
FINDINGS OF FACT
In October 2008, claimant sustained a compensable injury. (Exs. 1, 12). In
November 2008, the self-insured employer accepted a left knee strain. (Ex. 12).
A December 2008 Notice of Closure did not award permanent disability
benefits. (Ex. 15).
In December 2018, the employer accepted a left knee ACL tear condition.
(Ex. 77). In July 2019, the employer reopened claimant’s Own Motion claim for
a “post-aggravation rights” new/omitted medical condition (left knee ACL tear).
(Ex. 106).
1 Because claimant is unrepresented, he may wish to consult the Ombudsman for Injured
Workers. He may contact the Ombudsman, free of charge, at 1-800-927-1271, or write to:
OMBUDSMAN FOR INJURED WORKERS
DEPT OF CONSUMER & BUSINESS SERVICES
PO BOX 14480
SALEM OR 97309-0405
2 Claimant’s October 2008 claim was accepted as disabling and first closed on December 2, 2008.
(Exs. 12, 15). Thus, claimant’s aggravation rights expired on December 2, 2013. Therefore, when
claimant sought claim reopening in November 2018, the claim was within our Own Motion jurisdiction.
(Ex. 72); see ORS 656.278(1). On July 3, 2019, the Board issued an order authorizing claim reopening
for claimant’s Own Motion claim for a “post-aggravation rights” new/omitted medical condition (left
knee ACL tear). (Ex. 106). On July 23, 2020, the self-insured employer issued its Own Motion Notice
of Closure. (Ex. 115).

74 Van Natta 1 (2022) 2
A June 23, 2020, Own Motion Notice of Closure did not award any
permanent disability benefits for the left knee ACL tear. (Ex. 115). The closure
notice also indicated that claimant had been released to regular work. (Id.)
Claimant requested review of the Own Motion Notice of Closure on August 3,
2020. (Ex. 117).
In January 2021, we referred claimant’s Own Motion claim to the Director
to appoint a medical arbiter. See Sigurd N. Meland, 73 Van Natta 50 (2021).
In July 2021, Dr. Dekker performed a medical arbiter examination. She
noted the following range of motion (ROM) findings: 120 degrees flexion and a
5-degree extension deficit for his left knee; and 128 degrees flexion and 0 degrees
extension for claimant’s right knee. Dr. Dekker stated that claimant had extensive
arthritis in his left knee and chronic effusion and 4 degrees of varus deformity in
his left leg. In addition, she recorded that claimant did not have a history of right
knee injury or disease. Further, she opined that claimant was significantly limited
in the repetitive use of his left knee due to osteoarthritis that was partially caused
by the accepted ACL tear condition. Moreover, Dr. Dekker stated that 75 percent
of claimant’s impairment was related to the accepted ACL tear condition and 25
percent was related to osteoarthritis/degenerative changes. Finally, Dr. Dekker
concluded that claimant had grade 1 instability of the left ACL that was solely due
to the accepted ACL tear condition.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW AND OPINION
The claim was reopened for the processing of a “post-aggravation rights”
new/omitted medical condition (left knee ACL tear). Such a claim may qualify for
payment of permanent disability compensation. See ORS 656.278(1)(b); Goddard
v. Liberty Northwest Ins. Corp., 193 Or App 238 (2004).
We first determine whether ORS 656.278(2)(d) applies to limit any award
of permanent disability for the “post-aggravation rights” new/omitted medical
condition. The permanent disability limitation set forth in ORS 656.278(2)(d)
applies where there is (1) “additional impairment” to (2) “an injured body part”
that has (3) “previously been the basis of a [permanent disability] award.” See
Cory L. Nielsen, 55 Van Natta 3199, 3206 (2003). If those conditions are satisfied,
the Director’s standards for rating new/omitted medical conditions related to non-
Own Motion claims apply to rate “post-aggravation rights” new/omitted medical
condition claims. See Lynette M. Kertis, 73 Van Natta 690, 692 (2021). Under
such circumstances, we redetermine the claimant’s permanent disability under

74 Van Natta 1 (2022) 3
those standards before application of the limitation in ORS 656.278(2)(d). See
Jeffrey L. Heintz, 59 Van Natta 419 (2007); Nielsen, 55 Van Natta at 3207-08.
Conversely, where it is determined that the limitation in ORS 656.278(2)(d) does
not apply, the permanent disability for the “post-aggravation rights” new/omitted
medical condition is rated under the Director’s standards without
“redetermination” of disability. See Randy D. Boydston, 59 Van Natta 2360
(2007); Terry L. Rasmussen, 56 Van Natta 1136, 1140 (2004).
Here, not all of the ORS 656.278(2)(d) factors are satisfied. Specifically,
claimant has not received a prior permanent disability award for his left knee.
Therefore, the limitation on permanent disability benefits set forth in ORS
656.278(2)(d) does not apply. See Carol M. Aldrich, 64 Van Natta 2217, 2219
(2012). Consequently, claimant’s new/omitted medical condition is rated under
the Director’s standards without a “redetermination” of disability.3 See Boydston,
59 Van Natta at 2365; Rasmussen, 56 Van Natta at 1140.
Where, as here, a medical arbiter is used, impairment is established based on
the medical arbiter’s findings, except where a preponderance of the medical
evidence demonstrates that different findings by the attending physician, or
impairment findings with which the attending physician has concurred, are more
accurate and should be used. See OAR 436-035-0007(5); SAIF v. Owens, 247 Or
App 402, 414-15 (2011), recons, 248 Or App 746 (2012). Only findings of
impairment that are permanent and caused by the accepted compensable condition
may be used to rate impairment. See OAR 436-035-0007(1); Khrul v. Foremans
Cleaners, 194 Or App 125, 130 (1994). Absent a combined condition denial, the
carrier pays for the full measure (without apportionment) of the worker’s
permanent impairment if the impairment as a whole was caused in material part
by the compensable injury. See Caren v. Providence Health Sys. Or., 365 Or 466,
487 (2019); Judith L. Croce, 72 Van Natta 1057, 1060 (2020).
Here, the parties do not dispute that the findings of Dr. Dekker, the medical
arbiter, should be used to rate claimant’s permanent impairment. Thus, we rely on
Dr. Dekker’s findings to rate claimant’s permanent impairment.
3 Claimant’s claim was closed by a June 23, 2020, Own Motion Notice of Closure. Therefore, the
applicable standards are found in Workers’ Compensation Division (WCD) Administrative Order 20-051
(eff. March 1, 2020). See OAR 436-035-0003(1).

74 Van Natta 1 (2022) 4
Dr. Dekker noted the following left/right knee ROM findings: 120/128
degrees flexion and 5/0 degrees extension.4 In addition, because claimant’s right
knee does not have a history of injury or disease, a contralateral comparison is
appropriate. See OAR 436-035-0011(3). Therefore, claimant is entitled to the
following ROM values: 4 percent for flexion and 1 percent for extension.5 See
OAR 436-035-0220(1), (2). These values are added for a total leg (knee) ROM
impairment value of 5 percent. See OAR 436-035-0011.
Dr. Dekker also stated that claimant had extensive arthritis with chronic
effusion and 4 degrees of varus deformity. Consequently, claimant receives a
5 percent impairment value. See OAR 436-035-0230(11)(b).
Further, Dr. Dekker opined that claimant was significantly limited in the
repetitive use of his left knee. Therefore, claimant receives a 5 percent chronic
condition impairment value. See OAR 436-035-0019(1).
In addition, Dr. Dekker concluded that claimant had grade 1 instability of
the left ACL. Thus, he is entitled to a 5 percent instability value. See OAR 436-
035-0230(3).
There are no other ratable impairment findings. Therefore, we combine
claimant’s left knee impairment values as follows: 5 percent ROM loss, 5 percent
extensive arthritis/varus deformity, 5 percent chronic condition, and 5 percent
instability, resulting in a 20 percent loss of the left knee (leg). See OAR 436-035-
0011(6). The 20 percent loss of the knee (leg) is converted to 9 percent whole
person impairment. See OAR 436-035-0235(4).
In reaching the foregoing conclusions, we recognize that Dr. Dekker stated
that 75 percent of claimant’s impairment was related to the accepted ACL tear
condition and 25 percent to osteoarthritis/degenerative changes. However, the
4 Dr. Dekker found a 5-degree extension “deficit” for claimant’s left knee. Although she also
noted “(-5º),” we interpret Dr. Dekker’s 5-degree deficit finding to mean a 5-degree extension loss for
purposes of OAR 436-035-0220(2), which states that 0 degrees describes the knee in full extension. In
addition, Dr. Dekker did not indicate any hyperextension.
5 We compare claimant’s left/right knee flexion findings as follows: 120/128 = X/150; X =
140.6, which is rounded to 141 degrees. See OAR 436-035-0011(3), (4). 141 degrees receives a 3.6
percent impairment value, which is rounded to 4 percent. See OAR 436-035-0220(1); OAR 436-035-
0011(4)(a). We compare claimant’s left/right knee extension findings as follows: 145/150 = X/150;
X = 145; 150-145 = 5 degrees. See OAR 436-035-0011(3). 5 degrees receives a 0.5 percent impairment
value, which is rounded to 1 percent. See OAR 436-035-0220(2); OAR 436-035-0011(4)(a).

74 Van Natta 1 (2022) 5
employer has not denied a combined condition involving left knee osteoarthritis
or degenerative changes. (Exs. 15, 115). Absent a combined condition denial,
Dr. Dekker’s opinion establishes that claimant’s impairment as a whole was caused
in material part by the compensable injury. Under such circumstances, claimant is
entitled to the full value of his permanent impairment, without apportionment.
See Caren, 365 Or at 487 (the claimant was entitled to the full measure of her
permanent impairment where the carrier had not denied a combined condition and
the record established that the claimant’s impairment as a whole was caused in
material part by the compensable injury); Croce, 72 Van Natta at 1060 (absent a
combined condition denial, the medical arbiter’s opinion that attributed 20 percent
of the claimant’s impairment to the accepted condition and 80 percent to
preexisting arthritis established that claimant’s impairment as a whole was caused
in material part by the compensable injury).
Finally, because claimant was released to regular work, he is not entitled to a
work disability award. (Ex. 115); see OAR 436-035-0009(4); Kertis, 73 Van Natta
at 692 n 2.
In sum, based on the aforementioned reasoning, the record persuasively
establishes that claimant is entitled to a 9 percent whole person permanent
impairment award. The June 23, 2020, Own Motion Notice of Closure did not
award any permanent disability benefits. Accordingly, we modify the closure
notice to award 9 percent whole person permanent impairment for claimant’s
“post-aggravation rights” new/omitted medical condition (left knee ACL tear).
IT IS SO ORDERED.
Entered at Salem, Oregon on January 3, 2022
